title: Hail the King
reviewNotes: Complete seven-piece diagram after ...Rxc7 at 164 seconds re-reviewed. Source Rh8 mate claim corrected: ...Rh7 is the only legal interposition and Rxh7 is actual mate. Independent Rf7 loses. Earlier eight-piece king walk, queen offer and alternate king retreats remain outside exact verification.
transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players might make a draw, but only a true genius would be able to find the incredible [music] win that white has in this position. At first glance, this position seems completely [music] lost. Black has three pawns, and one of them is only two steps away from getting a new queen. But, white does have a resource. This pawn on A7 that is only one step away [music] from getting a new queen. But, unfortunately, there is a problem. If white simply tries to move this rook away, now after a G5 check, the king [music] is being attacked, and the rook opens an attack on the pawn. So, we are going to lose that pawn. But, white does have an interesting idea to keep the game going. The very precise rook to F8. At first glance, this doesn't seem to change anything. Black still has pawn to G5, and still we cannot take this pawn. We're just going to lose the other pawn. But, it is important to notice that a white has a more precise move. King to [music] F3. Well, what's the difference? We are still losing the pawn, right? Well, not exactly. White can play now rook to H8, and this is going to be a checkmate. So, actually black cannot pick up the pawn on A7, and has to keep trying to misplace the king. So, he gives another check, pawn to G4. It seems like white is going to be forced to relinquish the threats on the black king, and inevitably lose the pawn. But, now the black pawn is taking away an escape square of the black king. So, after king to F2, we are still threatening the checkmate with rook to H8. So, once again, black has to keep attacking this white king. Now, of course, it's pretty simple. We can come [music] back to F3, and recreate the threats with the king. But, here is where white realizes that black had a secondary plan. He managed to get the G pawn all the way down, one step away from promoting to a new queen. And indeed, after pawn to g2, if we promote to a new queen, black is also going to get a queen, and this is going to be a draw. Or at least you would think so. White starts with queen to c8 check. If the king goes up, there's going to be a forced checkmate starting with rook to f4. The king gets pushed, queen check, we collect the rook, and then we are going to win like this. But black is not that [music] naive, and instead of allowing this, he can simply go down, king to h2. And now there are no more checks. But sometimes chess defies all expectations. And in this position, white has the majestic queen to c7 check, sacrificing the queen completely. But of course, the queen cannot be touched. Rook h8 would be a checkmate, but this queen sacrifice is actually a fork, because if black moves the king instead, we are going to take the rook, and here another checkmate.
